title: never and exhaustive checking
description: Learn how the never type helps you catch missing cases and build truly exhaustive conditional logic in TypeScript.

data.text: The `never` type is one of the most misunderstood features in TypeScript. It represents the set of values that never occur. In practice, you rarely see `never` as the type of a variable. Instead, it becomes a powerful tool for enforcing exhaustive conditional logic, ensuring that every possible case is handled.

Every value is assignable to `never`, but `never` is assignable to every other type. That sounds backwards, but it is useful: it lets the compiler verify that a function always throws, always loops forever, or that a switch statement covers every case.

data.title: Functions That Return never

data.text: Imagine a React component that renders a button differently depending on the button state. If you use a union type for the state, you want the compiler to warn you when a new state is added but you forget to handle it. That is where exhaustive checking shines.

data.title: Exhaustive Switch Statement
data.content: Using never to catch missing cases

data.text: If someone later adds `'disabled'` to the `ButtonState` union but forgets to update the switch statement, TypeScript will show an error on the default branch because the new value can no longer be assigned to `never`.

data.title: Pattern for Exhaustive Checks
data.text: Create a reusable helper that forces every case to be handled. Many libraries and codebases define a small function like `assertNever(value)` so the pattern is consistent across the project.

data.title: Reusable Exhaustive Check Helper
data.content: A helper function for exhaustive checks

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: It is most useful in the default branch of exhaustive checks
Adding a helper like `assertNever` makes the pattern reusable
Exhaustive checks prevent bugs when union types change
data.takeaway: never turns union type changes into compile-time errors instead of runtime surprises.
